title: Learning to make games as a hobby/side gig with Claude. How do I level up?
author: MunWhatever
selftext:
Hey,  
  
I recently started to use Claude and a bit of Lovable to help me with my day work and I discovered one can build games with it also. I am not a developer, but I grew up playing a lot of PC and board games and this piqued my interest. I did start to work on some small projects by trial and error, but it feels like I should get a deeper knowledge about developing and games infrastructure in general.

For now I just want to do some simple 2D games for web and mobile, but I do want to give a chance to bigger projects that I have in mind. I feel like I  should just get to know more before committing myself to one.

A few questions for people further along:

1. **Setup:** for 2D games (browser + mobile), what stack/engine do you use with Claude? Phaser, Godot, something else?
2. **Workflow:** how do you work with Claude on bigger projects so things don’t fall apart? Planning docs, small steps, tests? Especially if I change direction mid project.
3. **Learning:** I don’t have a solid coding background. What should I learn so I actually understand more of what Claude is doing?
4. **Avoiding “AI slop”:** I don’t want to pump out low-effort AI games. For me AI is the tool that lets me finally turn my game ideas into something playable. What separates a game made *with* AI that feels thoughtful and polished from one that feels like slop? Where should I put my own effort so the result is actually good?

Any advice is much appreciated!

comments.author: Chocoweb88
comments.body:
I am at the same page, have no coding experience nor knowledge, and have no idea where to start. So what I do is I ask Claude for advice, ask it to compare and analyse what tools are more beginner friendly. And as I start build the game, I ask Claude to explain to me (with very beginner friendly terms and step by step guide) what are the things it does, and how do I do certain things, add certain mechanics, apply certain sounds or arts into the game, how to publish game etc, all these Claude can teach you.

Now here are the lessons I just learn last week: dont spend too much time build the "completed" version of a game. Build a prototype with only simple buttons, simple shapes, and test that the game is fun to play first. I thought I was working with a simple but unique card game that should be fun to play for some players, but then I got the feedback and wake up call that my game may be starting on the wrong idea and foundation (i worked on it for 1 year 😂)

But its still fun and good learning experience for me. I created my game with Unity and now has decent understanding how it works and how to publish games on mobile, all teached and guide by claude. Next step for me is try learn other tools and either redesign my first game, or build another prototype as a fresh start. 

Good luck and have fun!

replies.author: Chocoweb88
replies.body: 1 more thing, as for how to make the game fun and not slop, I am not in the position to share because I am still learning as well. I guess keep trying, keep researching and play other games, and share the early work for feedback is the way to do it. Claude can compare if your game has been made before, but in the end it is up to human to decide if a game is fun or not

replies.author: MunWhatever
replies.body: Thanks for the input! That's pretty much the direction I was going too. I started with something simple and then overcomplicated it. Complexity can be fun, but I think it's important to understand what I'm doing in more depth so I can actually polish and change things as I go. I feel like that's the point where AI starts fixing one thing and breaking another, if I'm not learning what it's actually doing.

replies.author: Chocoweb88
replies.body:
I am a noob at game design with no knowledge at all too, so the most important is we keep learning ourself and use AI as supporting tools!

And then there's also marketing and sharing your game for people to play... that i still have no idea how it works haha.

comments.author: HenryFromNineWorlds
comments.body:
You need to just treat your ai as a coder. Do not ask it for design advice and do not let it make any design decisions in terms of gameplay, otherwise you are not a designer and your game will be slop. 

You need to do game design, balancing, story, etc yourself. Ai just wires it all together and does code generation. 

Be disciplined.

replies.author: FondantIcy866
replies.body: I wish I had heard this sooner. And unfortunately I don't feel confident to do all that stuff on my own...I guess I thought the AI was all powerful, then spent two weeks realizing it wasn't.

replies.author: HenryFromNineWorlds
replies.body:
I mean, you yourself have to add value or else…what are you even doing right? You’re just a slop merchant meat proxy if the ai is doing it all.

Games are art, and art is made by humans. Game design is extremely challenging and requires study and effort. Ai cannot shortcut you there.

comments.author: Arkenhammer
comments.body: The way I would start is by going through a basic tutorial for how to make a game without AI and use that process to figure out how the AI can help you. The fundamentals of making a game are the same either way, it is just that AI can do some of the work for you.

replies.author: MunWhatever
replies.body: Makes sense, thanks. Is there a specific tutorial or engine you'd recommend starting with for that? I'd rather start with simple 2D single-player games so I can grasp what's happening, and snowball into larger projects from there.

replies.author: Arkenhammer
replies.body: I haven't gone through a tutorial in years. The one I learned from was the Sebastian Lague Platformer Controller for Unity 5 but that's really old now. If you want to learn Unity (the engine I use), the tutorials on the Unity Learn Site have a good reputation. I know Godot is popular for AI but I've not tried it so I don't know what to recommend there. Unreal is overly complex for 2D games so I wouldn't recommend that.

comments.author: Significant-Neck-520
comments.body:
A year ago I would try to check if the code generated was extensible, so I would request Gemini to produce code that was "production-ready", trying to avoid tech debt. I was already having a hard time keeping track of the code, though, and once I switched to Claude using Codex, I just gave up on looking at the code. Maybe this will bite me later, but so far I got to finish a demo for a small game - for larger games, I think tech debt could still accumulate.  
For learning, you ask Claude to explain to you what it is doing, or open a new session to ask for clarification on how everything works. If things get to complex, you can always ask for more and more clarification.  


Now, the problem with AI slop is that previously you would take 4 years to build a game, so you would be playing that game over and over again, checking what worked, what didnt, what parts you started to hate and decided to remove. Now that everything is done in a month you may not have time to properly polish the gaming experience. But I guess the way to fix this is to continue iterating over the product, even if it gets boring.

comments.author: olafthemanofsnow
comments.body:
Read books about game design. Watch videos about game design. Take courses about game design. Learn game design. Understand game design.

Then map it out. Learn how to create a game design document. And build the game piece by piece. 

More than happy to talk through my processes in more detail if its helpful.

comments.author: Infinite-One-9078
comments.body: Essayer, tester, se planter, essayer autrement,...
